title: Creative AI: Image, Video & Voice — Module Quiz

items.q: A diffusion model creates an image by:
options: Drawing elements one at a time in order
Starting from noise and repeatedly removing what does not match the description
Assembling fragments of training images
items.explain: The whole picture is shaped at once at every step, which is why its parts emerge together rather than in sequence.

items.q: Image models struggle with exact counts because:
options: Training images were poorly labelled
Nothing in the process counts — a number is a phrase shaping the whole image
Counting needs more computation than is available
items.explain: "Three cats" makes the image cat-ish in a three-ish way. There is no step at which objects are enumerated.

items.q: The most reliable way to keep text out of an image:
options: Write 'no text' in the prompt
Describe what you do want, such as 'a blank wooden sign'
Generate at a lower resolution
items.explain: Words pull the image towards what they describe, so naming text can summon it. A dedicated negative-prompt field works differently.

items.q: Which prompt slot is most often omitted, with the largest effect?
options: Subject
Composition and framing
Colour
items.explain: Where the camera sits and how the subject fills the frame changes the result more than almost anything else.

items.q: Words like 'stunning' and 'high quality' weaken a prompt because:
options: They are too long
They describe a judgement rather than anything visible
Models filter praise words out
items.explain: They pull towards the average of what the model associates with praise — usually over-saturated and slightly plastic.

items.q: Naming a medium such as 'watercolour' is powerful because:
options: It is rare in training data
It carries a whole set of visual conventions at once
It reduces the number of generations needed
items.explain: One word does the work of a paragraph. Omit it and a default glossy look is chosen for you.

items.q: Holding the seed constant while changing one word gives:
options: A completely different image
The same image with that word's influence changed
A higher-resolution render
items.explain: The seed is the starting noise. Fixing it turns generation into steering rather than rerolling.

items.q: Why change one variable per iteration?
options: Multiple changes render more slowly
Otherwise you cannot tell which change caused the improvement
Models ignore all but the first change
items.explain: You end up unable to reproduce a good result or reverse a bad one. Five deliberate iterations beat fifty rerolls.

items.q: When the composition is right but one small detail is wrong:
options: Reroll until that detail is correct
Fix it in an editor or inpaint just that region
Add 'perfect hands' to the prompt
items.explain: Rerolling a whole image to fix a corner is the most common way to lose a good result.

items.q: Image models can imitate a specific living artist because:
options: They retrieve that artist's work while generating
Their training data contained a great deal of that artist's work
Artists license styles to model providers
items.explain: Training collections were scraped from the public web and contained large amounts of copyrighted work, generally without consent or payment.

items.q: In most jurisdictions, copyright protects:
options: Particular works, not styles
Styles as well as particular works
Nothing produced with machine assistance
items.explain: That is why imitation of style is mainly an ethical question rather than a settled legal one.

items.q: Describing a look rather than naming an artist is practically better because:
options: It generates faster
It is more controllable, more distinctive, and survives model updates
It guarantees originality
items.explain: You adjust one property rather than hoping, and a name may silently stop working or work differently after an update.

items.q: Temporal consistency in video means:
options: A steady frame rate
Objects staying the same from frame to frame
Predictable generation time
items.explain: Nothing guarantees the coat stays the same colour, which is why drift and morphing are the characteristic failures.

items.q: Why plan a shot list rather than request a finished sequence?
options: Shot lists cost less to generate
Consistency degrades with length, and cuts hide drift
Models can only produce one shot at a time
items.explain: Short clips are cheap to reroll, and a deliberate sequence has a structure a generated 'video about X' lacks.

items.q: Which is most reliable with current video models?
options: A person speaking to camera
Short atmospheric b-roll with no people or text
One character across several shots
items.explain: Faces in motion, speech, text and character continuity are all where generated video still falls apart.

items.q: The difference between synthetic voice and voice cloning:
options: Cloning requires more computation
A synthetic voice belongs to nobody; a clone reproduces a specific identifiable person
Synthetic voices are lower quality
items.explain: The technology is similar. What differs is whether there is a real person on the other end of it.

items.q: Does a publicly available recording imply consent to clone that voice?
options: Yes, public material may be used freely
No — consent must be explicit, informed and specific to the use
Only for non-commercial purposes
items.explain: A podcast or lecture is public and is not permission to be synthesised. Permission for one use is not permission for another.

items.q: A practical caution about cloning your own voice:
options: It degrades the source recordings
It weakens voice authentication, and the samples act like credentials
Most providers prohibit it
items.explain: A good clone undermines systems that identify you by voice, so prefer another factor and protect the samples accordingly.

items.q: The test for whether generated media needs a label:
options: Whether it took several attempts
Whether a reasonable person would take it as a record of something that happened
Whether it is photorealistic
items.explain: A stylised illustration borrows no promise. A realistic image of a real place or person borrows the promise that someone was there.

items.q: Provenance metadata such as C2PA can:
options: Prove an untagged file is authentic
Show a claim was attached and has not been altered since
Detect whether any image was AI-generated
items.explain: It travels only with files carrying it and is routinely stripped by uploading and screenshotting, so absence proves nothing.

items.q: Disclosure belongs in a visible caption rather than only metadata because:
options: Metadata is hard to author
Metadata is commonly stripped on upload, so it may disclose nothing to anyone
Captions improve search ranking
items.explain: A caption survives a screenshot. Credentials that die on upload have told the viewer nothing.

items.q: The likeness test asks:
options: Whether the image is photorealistic
Whether they would recognise themselves, and agreed to this specific use
Whether the person is a public figure
items.explain: Both halves must hold, and recognition can come from a voice or a setting as much as a face.

items.q: Which of these is NOT a grey area?
options: Historical reconstruction for teaching
Sexual imagery of a real person without their consent
Satirical cartoons of politicians
items.explain: It is the most common serious harm from these tools and criminal in many jurisdictions. "Private" and "obviously fake" are not defences.

items.q: For satire, the workable distinction is:
options: Whether the subject is a public figure
Realism — obvious commentary differs from a realistic fabrication
Whether a label is attached
items.explain: A cartoon is unmistakably commentary. A photorealistic video is not, even labelled, because labels do not survive the third repost.
